documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
New patient, 56 y/o man transferring care.

He is here mostly to get set up. Feels well. Works as a logistics coordinator for a distributor, a lot of time at a desk and on the phone, some walking the warehouse floor. No chest pain, no breathing trouble with his usual activity, no swelling. Sleeps fine.

Oncology history as he tells it and as his paperwork shows: Hodgkin lymphoma stage II in 2003, staged with a laparotomy and splenectomy, treated with mantle field radiation, no recurrence since. Prostate adenocarcinoma Gleason 3+4 found in 2020; radical retropubic prostatectomy with pelvic node dissection in October 2020, then adjuvant external beam radiation in early 2021 with leuprolide, which urology has kept going. He gets the 7.5 mg injection there every 28 days and they check his PSA. Bone density at his old office earlier this year showed osteopenia, blamed on the hormone therapy; takes calcium with D twice a day.
Other: hypertension and high cholesterol for several years. Right hip scope around 2013.

Meds: amlodipine 5 daily, atorvastatin 20 daily, aspirin 81 daily, calcium carbonate 600 / D3 400 twice daily, leuprolide 7.5 mg IM q28 days (urology).
Allergies: penicillin (rash); shellfish (anaphylaxis, had a reaction years ago at a restaurant). Has never had an epinephrine pen.
Family: father prostate cancer at 72, now deceased; mother breast cancer at 68; maternal grandfather coronary disease.
Social: married. Former smoker, about 20 pack-years, stopped in 2017. A drink or two on weekends. PHQ-2 0.

Exam: BP and vitals per flowsheet. Well appearing. Healed midline and lower abdominal scars. Neck supple, no thyromegaly or nodes. Heart regular, no murmur or rub. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Legs without edema. Gait normal.

Assessment and plan:
1. HTN, controlled on amlodipine 5. Continue.
2. Hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 20. Fasting lipids today.
3. Prostate cancer on ADT, followed by urology. Asked him to have their letters copied to us.
4. Hodgkin survivor after mantle radiation and splenectomy. TSH today and yearly. Asplenic: PCV20 given today; meningococcal vaccines at next visit once old records confirm what he had in 2003.
5. Osteopenia on ADT: continue calcium/D; repeat DXA in about two years.
6. Shellfish anaphylaxis: epinephrine auto-injector prescribed, showed him how to use the trainer.
7. Lung screening: qualifies by pack-years and quit date. Low-dose CT ordered.
8. Hep C and HIV screening today. CMP, CBC, vitamin D.
Records release already sent. Follow-up in about 5 months.

Kidney and liver tests, blood counts and thyroid are normal, vitamin D is fine on what you take, and the hepatitis C and HIV screens were negative. LDL cholesterol is about 100 on atorvastatin, which is acceptable; we'll keep the current dose. The lung CT scheduling desk should call you this week.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Came in because his belt doesn't close anymore. Thinking back, his belly has been growing and his legs swelling since around April, slowly. Now winded on the stairs at work and walking the loading dock, which is new. No chest pain, no palpitations, no fainting. Not short of breath at rest. Still on amlodipine 5, atorvastatin, aspirin, calcium/D, leuprolide.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet; weight up about 3 kg since May. Neck veins look full sitting up. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen distended, soft, nontender. Pitting edema of both legs to mid-shin.

A/P
Six months of edema, abdominal distension and exertional dyspnea. This is more than amlodipine. With mantle radiation in 2003 I am concerned about a cardiac cause: radiation heart disease, pericardial or myocardial. Urgent cardiology referral today; their office can see him within a few weeks and will do echo there. Low salt in the meantime. To call or go to the ED if breathing worsens or chest pain.

medications.reason: constrictive pericarditis with edema and ascites

reports.text: PA and lateral chest. Curvilinear calcification along the pericardium, best seen on the lateral view. Cardiac silhouette normal in size. Lungs clear. No pleural effusion. No pneumothorax.

Technically adequate study. Left ventricle normal in size with normal wall thickness and normal systolic function. Right ventricle normal in size and function. The pericardium is thickened and bright. Mitral inflow and tissue Doppler show impaired diastolic filling. No pericardial effusion. Valves without significant stenosis or regurgitation.
reports.conclusion: Thickened pericardium with normal systolic function and impaired diastolic filling, concerning for constrictive physiology.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group. Consultation 10/09/2023.
Referring: primary care.
Patient: Howard Nadeau, 57 years old.

Reason: half a year of rising abdominal girth, leg swelling and exertional breathlessness.

HPI: Mr. Nadeau describes six months of slowly worsening swelling of the abdomen and legs and breathlessness with exertion. He has had no chest pain, palpitations or syncope.

Background: stage II Hodgkin lymphoma in 2003 with mantle field radiation and staging splenectomy, in remission. Prostate adenocarcinoma Gleason 3+4, radical prostatectomy 2020 then adjuvant external beam radiation, on leuprolide. Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, osteopenia on ADT. Right hip arthroscopy.
Medications: leuprolide 7.5 mg IM every 28 days; amlodipine 5 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg daily; calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 600 mg/400 IU twice daily; aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).
Family: father prostate cancer, mother breast cancer, maternal grandfather coronary disease.
Social: former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 2017. Alcohol 1 to 2 drinks weekly. Logistics coordinator.

Exam: BP 115/75, HR 88, RR 18. Jugular venous pressure elevated. A pericardial knock is audible in early diastole. Abdomen distended with a fluid wave. Liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin. Pitting edema 2+ in both legs to the knees. Lungs clear.

Data: Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.8, platelets 235, creatinine 1.1, albumin 3.5, ALT 45, AST 50, total bilirubin 1.2, BNP 150.
Chest x-ray: pericardial calcifications.
Echo: thickened pericardium, normal systolic function, impaired diastolic filling.

Impression: constrictive pericarditis, almost certainly a late effect of mantle radiation, with right-sided congestion (ascites, hepatic congestion, edema). The modest BNP fits constriction rather than myocardial failure.

Plan:
1. Start furosemide 40 mg every morning; BMP in one week (asked PCP to draw).
2. Cardiac MRI for pericardial thickness and ventricular interdependence.
3. Right and left heart catheterization to confirm constrictive hemodynamics and look at the coronaries before any surgery.
4. If confirmed, refer for pericardiectomy.
5. Continue other medications.
Thank you for the referral.
Outside cardiology

documents.title: Cardiac MRI report (outside)
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
Outside imaging center. Cardiac MRI with and without gadolinium, 10/30/2023.
Indication: suspected constrictive pericarditis after mantle radiation.
Findings: Pericardium diffusely thickened, up to 6 mm over the right ventricle. Septal bounce on cine imaging with exaggerated septal shift on free-breathing sequences, consistent with ventricular interdependence. LV normal in size, LVEF 58%. RV normal in size and function. No myocardial late gadolinium enhancement. Small ascites in the visualized upper abdomen. No pericardial effusion.
Impression: Findings consistent with constrictive pericarditis. Normal biventricular systolic function, LVEF 58%.

documents.title: Cardiac catheterization report (outside)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiac catheterization laboratory. Date 11/20/2023.
Procedure: right and left heart catheterization with coronary angiography, right radial and right femoral venous access. Allergies reviewed: penicillin, shellfish (anaphylaxis); no iodinated contrast reaction history; premedication not required.
Hemodynamics: RA 18 mmHg. RV end-diastolic 19 mmHg with dip-and-plateau waveform. PCWP 19 mmHg. LVEDP 20 mmHg. Near-equalization of diastolic pressures. Simultaneous LV/RV tracings show discordant respiratory variation of systolic pressures.
Coronaries: no obstructive coronary artery disease.
Conclusion: hemodynamics diagnostic of constrictive pericarditis. No obstructive CAD. Refer to cardiac surgery for pericardiectomy.
No complications; discharged same day.

documents.title: Video visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, he's in his car on lunch break, verified DOB.

Wanted to talk through the cardiac surgery recommendation. Reviewed with him: MRI 10/30 shows thickened pericardium 6 mm and normal pumping, LVEF 58%; cath 11/20 confirmed constrictive physiology and no blockages. Surgeon visit done; pericardiectomy planned for 1/16. On furosemide 40, swelling down and belt fits again, still winded on stairs. Weight 87-88 kg at home.

We talked about why surgery is offered, that recovery after radiation-related constriction can be slower, and what the first weeks look like. He feels clear about going ahead.

Plan: hold aspirin per surgeon's instructions before surgery. Keep taking amlodipine and atorvastatin. Urology aware; leuprolide timing coordinated with them. I'll see him after discharge.

reports.text: Specimen: pericardium, radical pericardiectomy. Gross: multiple fragments of tan-white, firm pericardial tissue up to 7 cm, with gritty calcified areas. Microscopic: dense hyalinized fibrous tissue with dystrophic calcification and sparse chronic inflammation. No granulomas. No malignancy identified.
reports.conclusion: Fibrotic, calcified pericardium consistent with constrictive pericarditis. Negative for malignancy.

documents.title: Discharge summary, cardiac surgery (outside)
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
Regional medical center, cardiac surgery service.
Admitted 01/16/2024. Discharged 01/23/2024.
Patient: Howard Nadeau, 58 y/o M.
Allergies: penicillin (rash); shellfish (anaphylaxis).

Diagnosis: constrictive pericarditis, radiation-associated (mantle field radiation 2003), confirmed by MRI and catheterization.

Procedure 01/16/2024: radical pericardiectomy via median sternotomy, phrenic nerve to phrenic nerve, without cardiopulmonary bypass. Thick calcified pericardium removed; immediate improvement in RV filling on TEE.
Pathology: fibrotic calcified pericardium, no malignancy.

Course: extubated the evening of surgery. Chest tubes out day 3. Brief diuresis IV, transitioned back to oral. Atrial rhythm sinus throughout. Walking the halls by day 4. Pain controlled with acetaminophen. Aspirin resumed day 2.

Discharge medications: furosemide 20 mg daily (reduced from 40), amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, calcium carbonate/vitamin D twice daily, leuprolide per urology schedule.
Sternal precautions 6 weeks, no driving 4 weeks. Follow up with cardiology in about 3 months and PCP in 1-2 weeks.

documents.title: Post-hospital visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Two weeks out from pericardiectomy (1/16, discharged 1/23). Discharge summary arrived 1/30 and reviewed.

He says the stairs are already easier than before surgery. Sternum sore when he coughs or rolls over, uses acetaminophen at night. Sleeping in a recliner the first week, now in bed. Appetite fine. Ankles mostly down. Taking furosemide 20 each morning.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, weight 84 kg, down 6 kg from September. Sternal incision healing well, no drainage or erythema, sternum stable. JVP not elevated. Heart regular, no rub. Lungs clear. Abdomen flat, no fluid wave. Trace ankle edema.

A/P
1. S/p radical pericardiectomy for radiation-associated constriction, recovering well. BMP and CBC today. Furosemide per cardiology, follow-up there in April.
2. HTN: BP fine on amlodipine plus the diuretic.
3. Return to desk work after cardiology clears; sternal precautions until early March.
Short-term leave paperwork completed for his employer.

documents.title: Emergency department record (outside)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED. Arrival 04/01/2025 11:10.
Patient: Howard Nadeau, 59 M.

CC: back pain and trouble walking.
HPI: Two weeks of lower back pain getting steadily worse, now with difficulty walking. Describes pins-and-needles in both legs. Has leaked urine several times over the last few days without warning. Known prostate cancer (prostatectomy 2020, radiation, on leuprolide), remote Hodgkin lymphoma, and constrictive pericarditis.
PMH/PSH: as above; pericardiectomy 2024; splenectomy; hip arthroscopy. HTN, HLD, osteopenia.
Meds: leuprolide 7.5 mg IM q28 days, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, calcium carbonate/vitamin D3 twice daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: penicillin - rash; shellfish - anaphylaxis.
Family: father prostate cancer, mother breast cancer, maternal grandfather CAD.
Social: former smoker 20 pk-yr, quit 2017; 1-2 drinks/week; logistics coordinator.

Exam: vitals as charted, afebrile. Uncomfortable with movement. Lower extremities with increased tone; patellar and Achilles reflexes 3+ bilaterally; Babinski positive on the left, downgoing on the right.

Labs: Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.8, platelets 250. Calcium 9.6. Alkaline phosphatase 120 (high). PSA 9.8 (high).

MRI spine (urgent): mass at T8 compressing the thoracic spinal cord. See radiology report.

ED course: dexamethasone 10 mg IV given. Neurosurgery and oncology consulted in the department.
Impression: metastatic spinal cord compression at T8, prostate cancer metastasis suspected.
Disposition: admitted to neurosurgery.

documents.title: MRI thoracic and lumbar spine (outside)
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
Regional hospital radiology. MRI thoracic and lumbar spine without and with contrast, 04/01/2025.
Indication: back pain, myelopathic signs, history of prostate cancer.
Findings: Enhancing mass centered in the T8 vertebral body and posterior elements with epidural extension, compressing the thoracic spinal cord at T8. No pathologic fracture with loss of height. Remaining thoracic and lumbar vertebrae with normal marrow signal. Conus normal in position and signal. Lumbar discs without significant stenosis.
Impression: T8 osseous mass with epidural extension compressing the thoracic cord, most consistent with metastasis.

medications.drug: acetaminophen 325 MG / oxycodone hydrochloride 5 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain, #30

reports.text: Specimen: T8 epidural and posterior element tumor, resection. Microscopic: metastatic adenocarcinoma in bone and soft tissue, cribriform and glandular pattern. Immunohistochemistry: tumor cells positive for PSA and NKX3.1.
reports.conclusion: Metastatic adenocarcinoma consistent with prostate primary.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Discharge summary, neurosurgery (outside)
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, neurosurgery service.
Admitted 04/01/2025 via ED. Discharged 04/09/2025.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).

Diagnoses: metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma, castration-resistant, presenting with T8 spinal metastasis and cord compression.

Procedure 04/02/2025: T8 decompressive laminectomy with resection of epidural tumor and posterior instrumented fusion T6-T10.
Pathology: metastatic adenocarcinoma, PSA and NKX3.1 positive, consistent with prostate primary.
Testosterone <20 ng/dL on leuprolide, so disease is castration-resistant.

Course: dexamethasone started in the ED and tapered off before discharge. Leg sensation and strength improved after surgery; incontinence resolved by day 4, voiding normally. PT: walking with a single-point cane, stairs with rail. Oncology and radiation oncology saw him inpatient.

Discharge medications: oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 one every 6 hours as needed (#30), acetaminophen as needed, amlodipine 5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, calcium/vitamin D, leuprolide per urology. Aspirin resumed post-op day 7.

Follow-up: radiation oncology to start post-operative radiation to T8 in about 4 weeks; medical oncology for systemic therapy; neurosurgery wound check 2 weeks; PCP 2-3 weeks.
Discharged home with home PT.

documents.title: Appointment cancelled
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Patient called from the hospital to cancel today's 3:40. He went to the ED yesterday for his back and was admitted; says they found something on his spine and he's having surgery. Message to PCP.

documents.title: Post-hospital call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called patient, home since 4/9. Walking with a cane around the house, home PT twice a week. Bladder working normally. Incision checked by neurosurgery's nurse, fine. Using the oxycodone mostly at night, acetaminophen days. No discharge paperwork has come to us. Records request faxed to the hospital's medical records office today for the discharge summary, operative note and pathology. Booked with PCP 4/29.

conditions.label: Malignant neoplasm of prostate
conditions.note: now metastatic to T8, castration-resistant (testosterone <20 on leuprolide), pathology 04/2025

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Post-hospital visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after admission 4/1-4/9. Discharge summary and pathology came 4/24 after our request; reviewed.

Summary: ED 4/1 with two weeks of worsening low back pain, leg tingling, trouble walking and urinary leakage; upper motor neuron signs; MRI showed a T8 mass compressing the cord. PSA 9.8 (undetectable through 2023; 0.2 last April). Underwent T8 decompression and T6-T10 fusion 4/2. Pathology metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma. Testosterone castrate, so castration-resistant.
I wrote him back on 3/22 about a week of back pain with acetaminophen and a visit; he went to the ED the day before it.

Today: back pain 3/10, sharper with standing long. Walking with cane outdoors, without it at home. Legs feel close to normal. No incontinence. Off oxycodone this week. Mood: scared but practical; asks good questions about what castration-resistant means.
Meds: amlodipine 5, atorvastatin 20, aspirin 81, calcium/D, leuprolide (urology). Allergies PCN, shellfish.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, weight 82 kg. Thoracic incision healed, no tenderness or drainage. Strength 5/5 in both legs. Gait steady with cane.

A/P
1. Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with T8 cord compression, s/p decompression and fusion. Radiation to T8 starts 5/5 per discharge plan; medical oncology appointment pending, they will discuss systemic treatment. Updated problem list.
2. Explained red-flag symptoms again: new weakness, numbness, bladder or bowel changes go straight to the ED.
3. HTN fine. Continue meds.
Follow-up in about 3 months, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Radiation oncology completion letter
documents.author: radiation oncology
documents.body:
Outside radiation oncology. Treatment summary.
Patient: Howard Nadeau.
Diagnosis: metastatic castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinoma, T8 metastasis with cord compression, status post decompression and T6-T10 fusion 04/02/2025.
Treatment: post-operative external beam radiation to T7-T9, 30 Gy in 10 fractions, 05/05/2025 to 05/16/2025.
Tolerance: mild fatigue, no interruptions.
Allergies: penicillin, shellfish.
Plan: medical oncology for systemic therapy. Follow-up here in 3 months.

documents.title: PSMA PET/CT report (outside)
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
Outside imaging center. PSMA PET/CT, skull base to mid-thigh, 05/20/2025.
Indication: metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, staging.
Findings: PSMA-avid lesion at T8 at the site of recent surgery and radiation, with hardware T6-T10. No other PSMA-avid osseous lesion. Prostatectomy bed without avid recurrence. No avid pelvic, retroperitoneal or thoracic nodes. No visceral lesions.
Impression: avid disease limited to the treated T8 site. No other sites of metastatic disease.

documents.title: Specialty pharmacy call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Specialty pharmacy called to review his med list before shipping enzalutamide 160 mg daily (4 x 40 mg), prescribed by his oncologist. They had our list from 4/29. No interactions of concern with amlodipine or atorvastatin per their pharmacist. We had no oncology note about this; left message for patient to bring his current med list and have oncology send their consult.

medications.sig: Take 4 capsules (160 mg) by mouth daily, per oncology
120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, given at oncology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up. Brought his med bottles.

Radiation to T8 finished 5/16 (letter received). PSMA PET 5/20: only the treated T8 site. Oncology started him in June on enzalutamide 160 mg daily and denosumab 120 mg injections every 4 weeks at their infusion room; he's had two. We never received the oncology consult; the specialty pharmacy called us in June. Leuprolide continues at urology.

Feels tired by mid-afternoon since enzalutamide, otherwise OK. Back ache 2/10, no leg symptoms, bladder and bowels normal. Walking without the cane now.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Incision well healed. Strength 5/5 legs. Gait normal.

A/P
1. mCRPC, T8 treated. Med list updated with enzalutamide and denosumab per patient and pharmacy. Records request to oncology. Calcium important on denosumab: continue calcium/D twice daily. CMP and CBC today.
2. Fatigue likely enzalutamide; he'll raise it with oncology.
3. HTN on amlodipine, fine today.
4. Osteopenia: denosumab now covers bone protection.
See in 4 months for physical; flu/COVID in October.

documents.title: Medical oncology follow-up
documents.author: medical oncology
documents.body:
Outside medical oncology. Visit 08/19/2025.
Diagnosis: metastatic castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 3+4 at prostatectomy 2020; adjuvant RT and ADT 2021); T8 metastasis with cord compression 04/2025, decompression and T6-T10 fusion, post-op RT 30 Gy/10 fx. PSMA PET 05/2025: T8 only.
Treatment: leuprolide (urology), enzalutamide 160 mg daily since 06/2025, denosumab 120 mg SC q4 weeks since 06/2025.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).
Interval: fatigue grade 1. No new pain. No falls.
PSA 1.2 ng/mL today (9.8 at presentation).
Assessment: good PSA response on enzalutamide.
Plan: continue. PSA monthly with us; restaging if rising. Dental check reminder on denosumab. Next visit 3 months.

documents.title: Fall vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Influenza and 2025-26 COVID given, one in each arm. Checked with oncology's nurse line first: OK to vaccinate on enzalutamide. Tolerated.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Physical.

Interval: oncology letter in August, PSA down to 1.2 on enzalutamide. Denosumab monthly at oncology. Leuprolide at urology. No back pain most days, no leg symptoms, bladder fine. Working full days again. Tired some afternoons. Flu and COVID done in October.
Meds: enzalutamide 160, denosumab q4wk, leuprolide, amlodipine 5, atorvastatin 20, aspirin 81, calcium/D. Allergies PCN, shellfish; epi pen current.
PHQ-9 4; says he is managing and talks things over at home.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Well appearing. Heart regular, no rub. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Spine incision healed. No edema. Strength and gait normal.

A/P
1. mCRPC per oncology, responding.
2. HTN, hyperlipidemia stable on same doses. Lipids, TSH, vitamin D today; oncology checks his CMP and CBC.
3. Annual lung screening CT: he'd rather skip it this year with everything else going on; revisit next year.
4. Colonoscopy due 2029. Vaccines current.
Follow-up in about 4 months.

documents.title: Emergency department record (outside)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED, 04/14/2026 06:50.
Patient: Howard Nadeau, 60 M.

CC: sudden severe low back pain, weak legs, cannot urinate.
HPI: Woke with abrupt, severe low back pain that has stayed constant; over-the-counter pain relievers did nothing. Both legs weak, unable to void since last night. Metastatic prostate cancer with a T8 cord compression treated last year; this feels like that episode, only faster.
PMH: metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (T8 decompression and fusion 04/2025, radiation); prior cord compression; constrictive pericarditis s/p pericardiectomy; Hodgkin lymphoma remote; HTN; HLD; osteopenia.
Meds: leuprolide, enzalutamide, denosumab, amlodipine, atorvastatin, calcium/vitamin D, aspirin 81.
Allergies: penicillin - rash; shellfish - anaphylaxis.
Social: former smoker, quit 2017; social alcohol; logistics coordinator.

Exam: vitals as charted. In obvious pain. Light touch and pinprick diminished below the umbilicus bilaterally. Strength 3/5 in both lower extremities. Rectal tone diminished. Bladder distended on scan; Foley placed.

Labs: Hgb 13.2, WBC 7.8, platelets 250, creatinine 1.0, BUN 14, calcium 9.8.
MRI spine (urgent): mass compressing the thoracic spinal cord. See report.

Course: dexamethasone 10 mg IV. Neurosurgery and radiation oncology at bedside.
Impression: cauda equina syndrome; recurrent metastatic thoracic cord compression.
Disposition: admitted to neurosurgery.

documents.title: MRI thoracic and lumbar spine (outside)
documents.author: radiology

Findings: Postoperative changes of T8 laminectomy and T6-T10 posterior fusion with susceptibility artifact. Recurrent enhancing epidural soft tissue at T8, compressing the thoracic spinal cord. Other vertebral bodies with normal marrow signal. Conus and cauda equina normal in appearance. No lumbar canal stenosis.
Impression: recurrent epidural tumor at T8 compressing the thoracic cord.

documents.title: Discharge summary, neurosurgery (outside)
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, neurosurgery.
Admitted 04/14/2026 from ED. Discharged 04/24/2026 to inpatient rehabilitation.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).

Diagnoses: recurrent metastatic epidural compression of the thoracic cord at T8 (ED impression cauda equina syndrome); metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.

Procedure 04/15/2026: revision posterior decompression at T8 with resection of recurrent epidural tumor; existing T6-T10 instrumentation intact.
Radiation: stereotactic re-irradiation to the T8 epidural disease, completed before discharge.
Course: dexamethasone, tapered off by discharge. Leg strength improving, 3+/5 by discharge. Foley remained in place. Oncology aware; systemic therapy to be reviewed after recovery.
Aspirin held peri-operatively, resumed day 6.
Discharge to inpatient rehab with Foley, PT/OT.

documents.title: Rehabilitation discharge summary (outside)
documents.author: physical medicine and rehabilitation
documents.body:
Inpatient rehabilitation facility. Admitted 04/24/2026, discharged 05/08/2026 home.
Diagnosis: recurrent metastatic thoracic cord compression, s/p revision T8 decompression and re-irradiation.
Allergies: penicillin, shellfish.
Progress: daily PT and OT. Foley removed day 4 with voiding trial passed; post-void residuals consistently under 100 mL thereafter. Bowel regular. Lower-extremity strength 4/5 bilaterally at discharge. Ambulates 150 feet with a rolling walker, supervision on stairs.
Discharge plan: home with rolling walker, shower chair; outpatient PT 2-3 times weekly. Follow up with neurosurgery, oncology and PCP.

documents.title: Home from rehab
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Patient called: home since Friday 5/8 after the hospital and then two weeks of rehab. Using a walker, PT starting this week. Bladder emptying on its own. Asked the hospital and rehab to send summaries; faxed requests to both today. Appointment with PCP 5/20.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Post-hospital visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
After admission 4/14-4/24 and inpatient rehab 4/24-5/8. ED record, MRI, hospital and rehab summaries all arrived 5/12 and reviewed.

What happened: sudden severe back pain, leg weakness and urinary retention; ED found a sensory level at the umbilicus, 3/5 legs, reduced rectal tone, and labeled it cauda equina syndrome; MRI showed recurrent tumor at T8 compressing the thoracic cord. Revision decompression 4/15 and re-irradiation. Rehab: catheter out, voiding with low residuals, 4/5 legs, walker.

Today: walking in with rolling walker. Back pain 4/10, acetaminophen helps. Bladder: going on his own, no leakage. Bowels regular. Mood low some days but sleeping and eating. Off work for now.
Meds per his list: enzalutamide 160, denosumab q4wk, leuprolide, amlodipine 5, atorvastatin 20, aspirin 81, calcium/D. Oncology visit is next week to talk about what's next.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, weight 79.6 kg. Incision healed. Strength 4/5 in both legs. Steady with walker.

A/P
1. Recurrent metastatic cord compression at T8, recovering. Outpatient PT. Same red-flag instructions.
2. mCRPC: oncology to decide next systemic treatment.
3. HTN: BP fine; continue amlodipine.
4. Problem list carries the ED's cauda equina syndrome label as given in the record.
Will see in about 2 months; call anytime.

documents.title: Medical oncology note
documents.author: medical oncology
documents.body:
Outside medical oncology. Visit 06/09/2026.
Diagnosis: metastatic castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinoma; T8 cord compression 04/2025 (decompression, fusion, 30 Gy/10) and recurrent T8 epidural compression 04/2026 (revision decompression, stereotactic re-irradiation).
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).
PSA 6.4 ng/mL on 05/26/2026, up from a nadir of 1.2 in 08/2025.
Assessment: progression on enzalutamide.
Plan: stop enzalutamide. Begin docetaxel 75 mg/m2 IV every 3 weeks with prednisone 5 mg by mouth twice daily; cycle 1 given today. Continue leuprolide and denosumab 120 mg q4 weeks. CBC before each cycle here. Counseled on neuropathy, infection risk and fever precautions; asplenic, so fever is an emergency.

medications.sig: 75 mg/m2 IV every 3 weeks, given at oncology
Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with docetaxel, per oncology

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up. Oncology note of 6/9 received 6/12.

Oncology: PSA 6.4 in late May, progression on enzalutamide; enzalutamide stopped and docetaxel every 3 weeks with prednisone 5 twice daily started 6/9. He's had three cycles (6/9, 6/30, 7/21). Leuprolide and denosumab continue.

How he's doing: tired for 3-4 days after each cycle, then better. Appetite OK. No fevers. Back pain 2-3/10. Still using the rolling walker outside the house. Bladder fine. Outpatient PT twice weekly. PHQ-9 4.

Meds reconciled: docetaxel q3wk and prednisone 5 BID added; enzalutamide removed. Amlodipine 5, atorvastatin 20, aspirin 81, calcium/D, leuprolide, denosumab, epi pen.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Alert. Mouth without sores. Heart regular, no rub. Lungs clear. No edema. Legs 4/5. Gait steady with walker.

A/P
1. mCRPC on docetaxel/prednisone per oncology. CBC and CMP today so I have a baseline here between their checks.
2. Asplenic on chemotherapy: reviewed fever plan, ED for temp 100.4 or higher.
3. HTN controlled. Hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 20.
4. Fall vaccines: will coordinate timing with oncology in September.
Call or message anytime.

documents.title: Friday's labs

documents.body: Howard, your blood counts and chemistry from Friday came back fine for where you are in treatment; nothing needs action from me. Oncology can see them too.

documents.title: Medical oncology update
documents.author: medical oncology
documents.body:
Outside medical oncology. Visit 08/11/2026, cycle 4.
Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer on docetaxel 75 mg/m2 q3 weeks with prednisone 5 mg twice daily since 06/09/2026; leuprolide and denosumab continued.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), shellfish (anaphylaxis).
Tolerating with fatigue. No febrile episodes. Cycle 4 given 08/11.
Plan: continue docetaxel; restaging after cycle 6.
